props.plain_english: Revenue scales with how many passengers or aircraft movements actually turn up. A soft quarter cannot be recovered later.

props.name: Regulated revenue reset
props.plain_english: The top line is set by a periodic administrative determination rather than by a market. When the settlement moves, the ratio moves with it and the borrower cannot price its way out.

props.name: Capital programme delivery
props.plain_english: A large regulated asset is permanently mid-programme. Spend is debt-funded, and whether it earns a return depends on the regulator allowing it into the asset base at the pace assumed.

props.name: Inflation indexation mismatch
props.plain_english: Revenue and debt service are both linked to published inflation indices - but not always the same index, and not on the same dates. When they diverge, the cover or gearing ratio moves for reasons nobody at the asset chose and nobody at the asset can hedge away.

props.manifestation: Passenger throughput drives both aeronautical and retail income, and feeds through to interest cover inside the same rolling window.
The price control settlement fixes the allowed yield per passenger, which IS the numerator of interest cover. A tighter determination caps cover for the whole control period, not for one quarter.
Debt drawn to fund the programme raises the senior interest bill immediately, while the traffic and the allowed return the spend is meant to unlock arrive later.

Regulated charges are index-linked and part of the senior platform is index-linked debt. When the index feeding revenue and the index feeding debt service diverge, or land on different dates, cover moves with no operational change at all.
The determination sets the rate at which the regulatory asset base rolls forward, and that base is the denominator of this ratio. A slower roll-forward lifts gearing on an unchanged debt balance.

Capex enters the regulatory asset base broadly as incurred, so debt-funded spend lifts numerator and denominator together and the first-order gearing effect is small. The bite is second-order: disallowed spend, or spend admitted to the base more slowly than it is drawn, raises the ratio.

The regulatory asset base is indexed and a large share of the senior debt is index-linked and accretes with the same family of indices. The ratio therefore moves on an index print alone, in either direction, before any cash has changed hands.

Granting development consent for the Northern Runway enables a major capital project to proceed, which over time could increase operating cash flows and thus improve interest cover, though near-term capex may temporarily pressure it.
Granting development consent for the Northern Runway enables future capacity expansion, which could improve revenue and EBITDA, thereby increasing interest cover.
Regulatory approval for a runway development does not directly change interest coverage ratios in the near term.
Granting development consent does not by itself alter senior debt levels or asset ratios.
Granting of development consent does not by itself alter senior debt levels or asset ratios.

Regulatory approval to proceed with the Northern Runway is likely to trigger significant debt-funded capital expenditure, increasing senior debt relative to assets and pushing the senior debt ratio upward.
Regulatory approval reduces project execution risk and supports asset value and earnings, lowering the senior debt ratio over time.
Granting development consent for the Northern Runway likely triggers capital expenditure, increasing senior debt and raising the senior debt ratio.
